prompt: What is the test of whether a runbook is any good?

choices.text: It is longer than ten pages
choices.why: Length says nothing about whether it works.
The author fills the gaps from memory without noticing.
Right: someone competent who has never touched the system, using only the page.

choices.text: It is in the company wiki
choices.why: Where it lives matters, but it is not the test.

prompt: What does a runbook move, according to the lesson?

choices.why: Right: from the night to a calm afternoon, made once, with time to think.
That is lesson 20.
That is a switchover.
That is the write-up's stance, lesson 22.

prompt: Match each part of a runbook scenario with what it says.

pairs.right: What the failure looks like when the system copes
How to see whether it coped
The visible state that ends the incident

prompt: Why does the lesson insist on commands written out whole, copied from a run that worked?

choices.why: Security is not the point.
They do not.

choices.text: It makes the runbook longer, so it looks complete
choices.why: Completeness is measured by use, not length.

choices.text: A paraphrase has to be translated under stress
choices.why: Right: "restart the node" is a sentence; patroni ~/patroni/pg2.yml is not.

prompt: Why should a number in a runbook say where it was measured?

choices.why: They change when the system changes, not on a calendar.
Right: "about 30 seconds, measured in the rehearsal" makes 50 a finding.
The reader needs it, at the moment of use.
Credit is not the purpose.

prompt: Why is the runbook's first page a script rather than text?

choices.why: Printing is not the reason.
Right: so it is right every time it runs; a page about the state goes out of date the day after it is written.
It can; it just goes stale.
It only looks.

prompt: In the lesson's run, which port did HAProxy's port 5000 lead to?

choices.why: etcd stores a few keys, never data.
HAProxy asks Patroni's REST interface.

choices.text: To show the clock is right
choices.why: The date line does that.
Right: nothing else on the page changes without it: no etcd, no leader key, no failover.

prompt: How does a runbook usually go wrong?

choices.why: Right: the things it names change and the steps still read well; a port moves, a standby is retired, and the page still says to connect.
That is rarer than it being wrong.
Length is not how they decay.
Formatting is the least of it.

prompt: How many of the runbook's addresses answered `runbook-check.sh`?
The check asks each address whether it answers with `pg____`, PostgreSQL's own tool for that question.
The check covers addresses. How are a runbook's steps checked?

choices.why: grep finds addresses, not whether a step works.
Patroni knows nothing about the page.
Right: somebody other than the author, in a rehearsal or a drill, and corrected the same day.
They can, by following them.

prompt: Why must a copy of the runbook live outside the systems it describes?

choices.why: They are shared widely.
The copies should be the same.

choices.text: So that it can be edited during the incident
choices.why: Edits come after, the same day.

choices.text: It is lost with them otherwise
choices.why: Right: a wiki on the failed database, or behind the failed sign-on, cannot be read.

prompt: How does the runbook handle the replication password?

choices.text: It prints it in plain text
choices.why: Then anybody with the page has the password.
Then nobody can follow the step.

choices.text: It names the password manager entry
choices.why: Right: and the break-glass way in when the usual one is down.

choices.text: It asks the reader to call the owner
choices.why: That is the dependency the runbook removes.

prompt: During a rehearsal, somebody says "I would just ask Ana here". What does the lesson make of that?

choices.why: Right: whatever Ana would answer belongs on the page.
It shows a gap.

choices.text: A reason to stop the rehearsal
choices.why: It is a finding, not an abort.
The point is not depending on her.

prompt: Put what the course's lessons give the runbook in course order.
hint: Copies, machinery, the night, the check.
items: The backups it points to (lessons 2 to 10)
The machinery its scenarios describe (lessons 11 to 21)
How it is used on the night (lesson 22)
trap: The order is the course's; the runbook uses all of them at once.

prompt: A team's runbook says "connect to the reporting standby and check its lag", with no address. What would `runbook-check.sh` find, and what does that mean?

choices.why: There is no address to try.
Right: a step with no address is invisible to it; the step itself needs a rehearsal, and an address written in.
It simply finds nothing.
It says nothing about the standby.
